# Preface {.unnumbered}

These notes cover the part of CS 585, Image and Video Computing, that deals with programming with images, as taught by Margrit Betke at Boston University in Spring 2024. On the course's [schedule page](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/) this block lists five sets of lecture notes, and we follow the first three. Lecture notes 1 is a short deck on the pitfalls of programming with images, by Diane Theriault and Margrit Betke ([Lecture notes 1](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-Program-with-Images-Pitfalls.pdf)). Lecture notes 2 is the January 30 lecture on skin colour, image differencing, template matching and image pyramids ([Lecture notes 2](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-cs585-template-matching-ncc-pyramids-Jan30.pdf)). Lecture notes 3 is a case study of the KidsRoom, an interactive story space built at the MIT Media Lab by Aaron Bobick and colleagues, which watched children play using little more than subtracted video frames ([Lecture notes 3](https://www.cs.bu.edu/faculty/betke/cs585/open/2024-kids-room.pdf)). The same block lists readings on image moments, binary image analysis and thresholding, with Chapter 3 of Horn's *Robot Vision* (MIT Press, 1986) as the textbook reference, and we lean on those throughout.

The slides are pretty terse (as slides should be), and a lot of the real content was said out loud or written on the board, so a student reading the PDFs a week later is basically left to reconstruct it on their own. So what I'm trying to do here is fill in that missing layer, which means that wherever a slide states a formula we derive it, and wherever a slide names an algorithm we write it out in Python and run it on a small example you can check by hand.

I'm assuming you can program, and that you remember a little bit of calculus and linear algebra, but not that you've ever opened an image file in code before. Everything is done with three libraries, NumPy for arrays, OpenCV for reading files (and a few other conveniences), and Matplotlib for looking at the results, so if you're starting from scratch, this is all you need.

```bash
pip install numpy opencv-python matplotlib
```

A quick word on how to read these notes. [Section 1.1](01-programming-with-images.html#sec-images) is about what an image actually is inside a computer, and it follows Lecture notes 1. It has most of the traps people fall into in their first week, so if you only read one section carefully, make it that one. [Section 1.2](01-programming-with-images.html#sec-binary) covers the background from the readings, where we turn grey images into black and white ones and then measure the shapes that show up (both lectures rely on this constantly, since a skin-coloured face and a moving child each end up as a blob). [Section 1.3](01-programming-with-images.html#sec-faces) follows Lecture notes 2 and hunts for a face, first by its colour and then by comparing the picture against a template, and [Section 1.4](01-programming-with-images.html#sec-motion) brings in time, starting from the image differencing in Lecture notes 2 and ending up in the KidsRoom of Lecture notes 3.

One last remark. A lot of the methods here are old (some of them are from the 1970s), and most modern systems would just hand these jobs to a neural network, which is fine, but these are the ideas that the networks are quietly rediscovering anyway, and they're also the tools you end up reaching for at two in the morning when you need something that works on a webcam and you don't have any training data at all.

::: {.callout-note}
## Running the code in these notes

Every Python cell in this book was run when the page was built, so the output is already there to read. Each cell also has a *Run* button. The first time you press one, the page downloads Python together with NumPy, OpenCV and Matplotlib (about 35 MB, which your browser then keeps) and runs the code right in the page. Nothing needs installing. You can edit any cell and run it again, and your output replaces the printed one.

Python in the browser is slower than on a laptop, and some packages, PyTorch among them, are not available there. For those, run the code on your own computer instead. Download `start_kernel.py` and `requirements.txt` from the [course page](../), install the packages with `pip install -r requirements.txt`, and run `python start_kernel.py`. It opens this book connected to Python on your machine.

:::
